pages.x: In 1540 Pedro de Valdivia, a veteran of the conquest of Peru, marched south across the Atacama desert with about 150 Spaniards and many more native carriers. In February 1541 he founded Santiago. Within months the chief Michimalonco attacked and burned the new town, and the Spaniards held on only by a desperate fight.

In 1550 Valdivia pushed south into the lands of the Mapuche, a free people of farmers and herders who had no king and had never been ruled by the Inca. He founded Concepción, then more towns and forts beyond the Biobío river, and gave the conquered people to his men to wash gold in the rivers. Many died of overwork and new diseases.

Lautaro, a Mapuche youth, had been taken to serve as Valdivia's groom, and watched how the Spaniards fought and cared for their horses. He escaped and taught his people to fight in waves, one squadron relieving another until the horsemen tired. In December 1553 at Tucapel they wiped out Valdivia's column, and the governor was killed.

Lautaro beat the Spaniards again at Marihueñu in 1554 and forced them to abandon Concepción. In 1557 he marched north to free the peoples around Santiago, but by the Mataquito river a Spanish force fell on his camp at dawn. Lautaro was killed, still in his early twenties.

Spain sent a new governor, García Hurtado de Mendoza, with fresh troops by sea. In 1558 the war leader Caupolicán was captured and put to death at Cañete, impaled on a stake, a horror the Spaniards meant as a warning. It did not end the war. When one Mapuche leader fell, another was chosen to take his place.

A young Spanish soldier, Alonso de Ercilla, fought in these campaigns and wrote an epic poem about them, La Araucana, printed from 1569. He praised the courage of the Mapuche as much as that of his own side. It was the first great epic poem about the Americas, and it made Lautaro and Caupolicán heroes in Europe.

In December 1598 the war leader Pelantaro ambushed Governor Martín García Óñez de Loyola at dawn at Curalaba, and killed him and nearly all his men. A great rising followed. Within six years every Spanish town between the Biobío and the island of Chiloé, from La Imperial to Valdivia and Osorno, had been destroyed or abandoned.

To hold a line of forts along the Biobío, Spain had to keep a paid standing army in Chile, rare in its empire, and raids for slaves went on across the river. In 1641, at the parliament of Quillín, the governor and the Mapuche chiefs agreed that the Biobío would be the border, and that the Mapuche south of it were free.

The frontier held for two more centuries, with trade, missions and regular parliaments as well as raids. The Mapuche kept their land until Chile and Argentina conquered it in the 1880s. Today they are the largest native people of Chile, and Lautaro is honoured as a national hero.
pts: More than a century of war
Their land stayed free until the 1880s
